question: Do trained classifiers reduce within-class relative to between-class scatter at an approximately constant multiplicative rate across layers, and does that pattern justify architecture, robustness, and generalization guidance?

key_findings.claim: The paper reports nearly linear log separation-fuzziness curves across depth for several image classifiers.
key_findings.evidence: It defines D_l = Tr(SSw SSb^+) on training representations and fits D_l approximately rho^l D_0. Feed-forward networks, modified AlexNet/VGG, ResNet blocks, and DenseNet blocks often have displayed Pearson correlations near -1; rho is explicitly allowed to vary with depth, data, epoch, architecture, and hyperparameters.

key_findings.claim: The experiment-selection rule makes the headline straightness partly a selected outcome rather than an unbiased prevalence estimate.
key_findings.evidence: For each optimizer, the supplement tries five or seven learning rates and retains the trained model with the best equi-separation law at the final epoch. Correlations are then computed over only 4-20 layer/block points, without seed-level confidence intervals, residual diagnostics, a preregistered goodness threshold, or correction for this selection.

anchors.section: SI Methods: feedforward-network training and learning-rate selection

key_findings.claim: Separation fuzziness is blind to within-class variation outside the class-mean span and is unstable when between-class rank changes.
key_findings.evidence: SSb has rank at most K-1, so SSb^+ annihilates directions outside its range: within-class noise in those directions contributes zero to Tr(SSw SSb^+). The pseudoinverse also changes discontinuously when singular values cross zero. Thus a lower D need not mean globally tighter or more classifiable features, and layerwise changes in rank can masquerade as progress.

key_findings.claim: D is not a representation-invariant signal-to-noise quantity in the singular regime used here.
key_findings.evidence: With SSb singular, a general invertible non-orthogonal reparameterization does not make the Moore-Penrose inverse transform by A^{-T} SSb^+ A^{-1}. Consequently identical linear decision information can receive a different D after anisotropic feature scaling. Width, rank, batch normalization, and the choice of pre/post-activation checkpoint can therefore change the plotted law without changing the classifier function.

anchors.section: Discussion of nonlinear transformations and batch normalization

key_findings.claim: The layerwise law is sensitive to how a module boundary is chosen.
key_findings.evidence: A scalar is plotted per layer for feed-forward networks but per residual or dense block for modern architectures; mixed ResNet blocks even contain different numbers of layers. BERT features are an explicit failure case. Without testing alternative block partitions or random/untrained networks, near-linearity cannot distinguish a universal computational law from a coarse-graining and normalization artifact.

key_findings.claim: The proposed robustness result assumes the property it needs at the level of ratio perturbations and does not establish robustness to weight shifts.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 1 adds the same epsilon to every layer ratio D_l/D_{l-1} and applies AM-GM to a first-order product expansion. The authors acknowledge equal perturbations are improbable. No relation maps a norm-bounded weight perturbation to equal ratio changes, and no corruption, adversarial, calibration, or model-shift experiment measures predictive robustness.

key_findings.claim: The out-of-sample evidence is one confounded, low-accuracy comparison rather than validation of equi-separation as a generalization diagnostic.
key_findings.evidence: On one 20-layer CIFAR-10 FNN, standard training gives 23.85% test accuracy and correlation -0.997, while a two-stage frozen procedure gives 19.67% and -0.971; both fit training data perfectly. The intervention changes optimization and features simultaneously, has no repeated-run uncertainty, and tests only a 4.18-point difference between weak classifiers.

key_findings.claim: The architecture recommendations are substantially narrower than their presentation suggests.
key_findings.evidence: The claimed optimal depths of 6, 10, and 12 for MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 come from selected small feed-forward networks, usually on 1,000 balanced training images with 28x28 images reduced to 10x10. Width and shape advice likewise comes from eight-layer FNN sweeps. Accuracy, compute, calibration, and modern architecture baselines are not optimized jointly.

key_findings.claim: Later intermediate-collapse evidence directly contradicts the interpretation that all layers make equal progress.
key_findings.evidence: The closest subsequent larger-scale study reports layer inequality: deeper layers contribute much more to collapse and generalization, middle layers can be redundant, and convolutional and Transformer depth behave differently under memorization. This supports progressive separation but not equal multiplicative contribution as a general law.

anchors.section: Claim that each layer becomes roughly equally capable

key_findings.claim: The evidence supports a useful exploratory layerwise diagnostic, not a universal law or validated design principle.
key_findings.evidence: The recurring monotone reduction is consistent with progressive neural collapse and representation simplification. Universality is limited by BERT failure, batch-normalization dependence, post-selection, small data, metric degeneracies, flexible module grouping, and the absence of held-out predictive tests for the architecture and robustness claims.

method.core_idea: Measure a trace ratio of within-class scatter to the pseudoinverse of between-class scatter at each hidden representation and test whether its logarithm is affine in layer or block index.
method.mechanism: Train image classifiers to interpolation, collect training activations at selected module boundaries, compute D_l = Tr(SSw,l SSb,l^+), and fit a constant geometric decay. Use sweeps over depth, width, optimizer, epoch, data, and architecture to illustrate recurrence, then derive heuristics from the fitted curves.
assumptions: The singular trace ratio faithfully measures all class-relevant separation.
D values are comparable across representations of different width, rank, normalization, and scale.
Layer or block index is a canonical unit of computation.
Selecting hyperparameters for best equi-separation does not bias prevalence or fit quality.
High Pearson correlation across a small number of modules establishes a geometric law.
Training-representation geometry predicts held-out accuracy, robustness, and architecture quality.
Uniform additive perturbations of all separation ratios approximate actual weight perturbations.

techniques.role: Summarizes within-class scatter relative to the pseudoinverse between-class scatter.
Operationalizes equi-separation through correlation of log D with module index.
Shows when the fitted layerwise pattern emerges during prolonged interpolation training.
Uses D curves to motivate architecture heuristics.
Treats layers in FNNs and blocks in residual/dense networks as comparable x-axis units.

evaluations.setting: 4-, 8-, and 20-layer ReLU FNNs on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 under SGD, momentum, and Adam
evaluations.metric: Pearson correlation between layer index and log D, plus final D
evaluations.result: Selected runs commonly report correlations from about -0.997 to -1 and geometric-looking decay, especially after prolonged training.
evaluations.baseline: Different depths, optimizers, learning rates, widths, and epochs; no null/random-feature calibration.

evaluations.setting: Modified AlexNet/VGG and residual/dense convolutional networks on small image datasets
evaluations.result: Mostly monotone log-linear curves are displayed when conv layers or whole blocks are used as modules.
evaluations.baseline: Architecture comparisons with different, author-chosen module granularity.

evaluations.setting: 20-layer CIFAR-10 FNN, standard versus two-stage frozen training
evaluations.metric: Training loss/accuracy, test accuracy, and log-D correlation
evaluations.result: Both reach 100% train accuracy; standard obtains 23.85% test and -0.997 correlation versus 19.67% and -0.971 for frozen training.
evaluations.baseline: Frozen last 10 layers then frozen first 10 layers.

evaluations.setting: Fine-tuned BERT-base on 1,000 binary sentiment examples
evaluations.metric: D for CLS and average-pooled token representations across layers
evaluations.result: The supplement explicitly reports that the equi-separation law does not occur.

limitations: Learning-rate/model selection explicitly favors the best final equi-separation fit.
Most FNN experiments use only 1,000 balanced training examples and heavily downsampled images.
The metric ignores within-class variance outside the between-class mean span and is rank-sensitive.
The singular pseudoinverse ratio is not invariant to general invertible feature reparameterizations.
Module granularity changes by architecture and is not stress-tested.
Correlations use few depth points with no uncertainty, residual, or nonlinear model comparison.
Batch normalization is important to emergence but no normalization-matched null explains its role.
Robustness is an idealized ratio perturbation argument with no predictive robustness experiment.
Generalization evidence is one weak, confounded CIFAR comparison.
BERT is a reported counterexample, sharply limiting universality.
No code-level replication or independent holdout of the law is supplied in this review.
failure_modes: Between-class covariance loses rank and D falls despite lost class distinctions.
An anisotropic but invertible feature scaling changes D while preserving linear decisions.
Batch normalization mechanically equalizes layer scales and produces an apparently geometric curve.
Choosing larger blocks smooths a nonlinear layerwise trajectory into a straight line.
A high correlation over four or eight modules hides a systematic curved residual pattern.
Hyperparameter search finds a near-linear realization even when typical runs do not obey the law.
Training D improves while test separation, calibration, or subgroup performance deteriorates.
Noisy labels drive training collapse and memorization while held-out generalization worsens.
A Transformer distributes class information in directions and tokens that the chosen pooled metric misses.
reusable_insights: Layerwise geometry should be evaluated on held-out data and tied prospectively to predictive outcomes.
Representation metrics need invariance, rank-degeneracy, and null-model audits before being treated as laws.
Compare affine, curved, piecewise, and depth-dependent fits with seed-level uncertainty rather than relying on Pearson correlation.
Predeclare module boundaries or test conclusions across every reasonable coarse-graining.
Separate progressive class compression, exact equal-rate compression, and terminal neural collapse as distinct hypotheses.
Validate architecture heuristics against compute-matched accuracy and robustness, not against the same diagnostic used to propose them.
Perturb weights directly and estimate layerwise causal sensitivities instead of assuming equal changes in derived ratios.
open_questions: How often does equi-separation survive preregistered hyperparameters and unseen seeds?
Can an affine-invariant, rank-robust separation measure recover the same layerwise pattern?
Does the law hold on held-out, corrupted, long-tailed, or subgroup-stratified examples?
Which aspects are caused by batch normalization, ReLU, cross-entropy, or terminal-phase interpolation?
Are layer contributions equal after controlling for parameter count, FLOPs, residual path length, and block size?
Can early D trajectories prospectively select depth or stopping time better than validation loss?
Do direct weight perturbations show greater robustness when fitted ratios are equal?
What explains the BERT failure, and do modern vision/language Transformers exhibit layer inequality rather than equi-separation?
How do label noise and large class counts affect rank, pseudoinverse stability, and apparent collapse?

competitive_landscape.title: Prevalence of Neural Collapse during the terminal phase of deep learning training
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational terminal-phase class-geometry phenomenon used as the reviewed paper's endpoint comparison.
competitive_landscape.difference: Papyan et al. characterize last-layer within-class collapse, simplex class means, classifier alignment, and nearest-center decisions. Equi-separation instead claims a specific geometric rate throughout intermediate layers, a stronger and less invariant statement.

competitive_landscape.title: Nearest Class-Center Simplification through Intermediate Layers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior intermediate-layer neural-collapse and class-center simplification evidence.
competitive_landscape.difference: Ben-Shaul and Dekel study nearest-center mismatch through depth in vision and language models and propose an explicit variability-simplification loss. The reviewed work's distinct contribution is the constant geometric-rate hypothesis, not the discovery that class geometry progressively simplifies.

competitive_landscape.title: Feature learning in deep classifiers through Intermediate Neural Collapse
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest contemporaneous broad empirical study of covariance evolution across layers.
competitive_landscape.difference: Rangamani et al. measure progressive within/between covariance, weight-subspace alignment, and nearest-center behavior. Their evidence supports monotone intermediate collapse, while equi-separation adds the narrower claim that log progress is evenly distributed by layer.

competitive_landscape.title: Are Neurons Actually Collapsed? On the Fine-Grained Structure in Neural Representations
competitive_landscape.relationship: Counterpoint showing trace-level collapse can hide task-relevant residual structure.
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang et al. recover fine-grained subclasses from residual variation even when conventional collapse metrics are small. This warns that a scalar D trajectory cannot by itself describe all information preserved or lost through layers.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Neural Collapse Is Provably Optimal for the Deep Unconstrained Features Model
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later theory for collapse propagation across nonlinear layers.
competitive_landscape.difference: Sukenik et al. prove deep collapse at the global optimum in a binary deep unconstrained-features model. That result concerns idealized optimum geometry and does not imply constant empirical D ratios, architecture guidance, or the reviewed robustness proposition.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural collapse vs. low-rank bias: Is deep neural collapse really optimal?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later theoretical and empirical qualification of deep-collapse optimality.
competitive_landscape.difference: Sukenik et al. show that beyond two layers or two classes, regularization's low-rank bias can beat deep neural collapse in the standard unconstrained-features model. It reinforces the need to monitor rank rather than interpreting falling pseudoinverse-based D as unambiguously better separation.

competitive_landscape.title: Are all layers created equal: A neural collapse perspective
competitive_landscape.relationship: Most direct later test of equal layer contribution on larger architectures and harder data.
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhou et al. report layer inequality, depth-dependent redundancy, and architecture-specific memorization behavior on clean and noisy data. Progressive collapse persists, but their findings directly temper the reviewed claim that every module becomes equally capable of reducing fuzziness.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first quantitative geometric law for intermediate-layer data separation: every layer reduces separation fuzziness by an approximately constant factor, yielding practical guidance for architecture, robustness, generalization, and interpretation.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Prior and contemporaneous neural-collapse work already established progressive within-class compression and between-class dominance across layers. The genuinely distinct element is fitting a single exponential-by-depth curve and using its equality condition to motivate design claims. The paper demonstrates that visual pattern across selected small-data runs and several architecture families but provides no invariant metric, unbiased prevalence estimate, or prospective outcome validation.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Novelty is moderate as an interpretable empirical regularity and low as a universal law. Later primary work finds unequal layer contributions on larger/noisy settings, while metric rank and reparameterization failures leave open whether the striking straight lines reflect learning, normalization, selection, or coarse-graining. Architecture and robustness conclusions remain hypotheses rather than established consequences.

reviewer_notes: Read all 14 extracted pages, including SI protocols, architecture details, frozen-training comparison, BERT counterexample, and learning-rate selection. The audit checked the singular scatter metric algebra, module granularity, selection bias, correlation evidence, robustness derivation, and out-of-sample claims. Primary PNAS, PMLR, and NeurIPS competitors were checked through 2026-08-23. No numerical reanalysis of activations or code replication was performed.
